questions.q: What is a 'possession' of a section?
options: Buying the land beside the track
The section is formally handed over for maintenance work, with train running suspended or controlled within it
A train standing in the section
Possession of a passenger's ticket
questions.explain: Possession means protected, time-bound control of the track for work — not ownership of land.

questions.q: What is the exam name for the full possession process taught in the book?
options: General duty roster
Caution order working
Engineering Possession with Traction Isolation and Permit to Work (PTW)
Token block working
questions.explain: Plan, possession, isolation, earthing and Permit to Work (PTW) together form this named process — process-order questions are guaranteed on it.

questions.q: What is the correct order for safe work on track under live Overhead Equipment (OHE) territory?
options: Isolate the power, earth the OHE, then issue the Permit to Work
Permit to Work, isolate, earth
Earth, permit, isolate
Switch off, start work, earth later
questions.explain: Power off, then earthed dead, then the paper permission — reversing any two can kill.

questions.q: Earthing of the Overhead Equipment (OHE) comes at which point?
options: Before isolation
After the work is finished
Only if staff ask for it
After isolation and before the Permit to Work is issued
questions.explain: Isolation alone does not make a wire safe; earthing proves it dead, and only then is the Permit to Work (PTW) issued.

questions.q: Until what point must Overhead Equipment (OHE) be treated as LIVE?
options: Until trains stop running
Until night falls
Until it is formally isolated, earthed and covered by a permit
Until staff wear gloves
questions.explain: This is the most repeated safety line in railway exams: Overhead Equipment (OHE) is live until isolated, earthed and permitted.

questions.q: What is the FIRST stage of a possession?
options: Planning — the work is planned and the possession requested and approved in advance
Staff entering the track
Restoring the power
Running the first train
questions.explain: Possessions are planned in advance: place, time, limits, staff and protection are approved before anything happens.

questions.q: Who grants possession of a section?
options: The station announcer
Any supervisor on site
The train operator
Operations Control Centre (OCC) (the Traffic Controller), for a defined section and a defined time
questions.explain: Operations Control Centre (OCC) grants possession after the last train clears, for exact limits and an exact time window.

questions.q: Before possession is granted, what must happen to the section?
options: The first train must enter it
The last train must clear the section
Passengers must be detrained onto it
Power must be restored
questions.explain: Possession is taken only after the last train has cleared the section being handed over.

questions.q: Who takes possession on site and controls the worksite?
options: Any fitter present
The designated Person-in-Charge (PIC)
The power controller
A contractor's labourer
questions.explain: The Person-in-Charge (PIC) takes possession from Operations Control Centre (OCC), receives the Permit to Work (PTW) and controls all staff and tools inside the limits.

questions.q: When the Person-in-Charge (PIC) takes possession, the limits are made certain by:
options: A verbal guess
A notice on the board
Confirmation by repeat-back and logging of the limits
The PIC's memory alone
questions.explain: Limits confirmed by repeat-back and logged — the same discipline as every safety-critical instruction.

questions.q: Protection of a possessed section includes:
options: Signals/blocks set to stop trains entering, with scotches/stop boards as prescribed
Opening all signals to clear trains faster
Removing all stop boards
Leaving signals as they were
questions.explain: The section is physically and signal-wise sealed: signals at danger, blocks applied, scotches/stop boards placed.

questions.q: If the work can foul the adjacent line, what extra care is needed?
options: None — only the work line matters
Trains on the adjacent line are sped up
The adjacent line is ignored
Precautions for the adjacent line as prescribed, so that line is protected too
questions.explain: Work that can foul a neighbouring line extends the protection thinking to that line as well.

questions.q: Who switches off the traction power for the section?
options: The Person-in-Charge (PIC) personally at the wire
Any staff with a key
The Power Controller, through Supervisory Control And Data Acquisition (SCADA)/switching arrangements
The station master
questions.explain: Isolation is done by the Power Controller remotely through Supervisory Control And Data Acquisition (SCADA)/switching — not by worksite staff at the Overhead Equipment (OHE).

questions.q: Power isolation for the section means:
options: Traction power is isolated for that section and earthing devices are then applied
Only the station lights are switched off
The whole city's power is cut
Trains run on battery instead
questions.explain: Isolation plus earthing: the section's Overhead Equipment (OHE) is switched off, then short-circuiting/earthing devices are applied.

questions.q: The Permit to Work is issued to whom?
options: Every labourer individually by Operations Control Centre (OCC)
The train operator
The station announcer
The Person-in-Charge (PIC) of the worksite
questions.explain: The Permit to Work (PTW) ties a named person — the Person-in-Charge (PIC) — a named section and a named time together.

questions.q: What are the three things that must ALL be present before staff work on the Overhead Equipment (OHE) section?
options: Gloves, boots and a torch
Isolation, earthing and a Permit to Work
A supervisor, a flag and a whistle
Power, permission and passengers removed
questions.explain: Isolation + earthing + permit — all three, in that logic. Missing any one makes the work unsafe and unlawful.

questions.q: During the work stage, who may be inside the possession limits?
options: Any staff member who is curious
Only authorised staff, with tools and materials accounted for
Passengers taking a shortcut
Unauthorised contractors
questions.explain: Only authorised staff inside; every tool and material is accounted for so nothing is left on the track.

questions.q: Why is a lookout/safety watch posted during work where required?
options: To count the tools
To make tea for the staff
To warn staff of approaching danger, such as a movement on an adjacent line
To speak to passengers
questions.explain: The lookout's only job is watching for danger and warning the gang in time.

questions.q: During possession, communication must be maintained between:
options: The worksite (Person-in-Charge (PIC)) and Operations Control Centre (OCC)
The worksite and passengers
The PIC and the canteen
Nobody — silence is required
questions.explain: A communication check with Operations Control Centre (OCC)/Person-in-Charge (PIC) is maintained throughout the work.

questions.q: What is the correct order of the six possession stages?
options: Work → Planning → Protection → Hand-back → Isolation → Possession
Protection → Work → Planning → Isolation → Hand-back → Possession
Isolation → Planning → Work → Possession → Hand-back → Protection
Planning → Taking possession → Protection → Power isolation → Work → Hand-back
questions.explain: Learn this order cold: plan it, take it, protect it, isolate it, work in it, hand it back.

questions.q: What must the Person-in-Charge (PIC) do before handing back the possession?
options: Simply walk away when time ends
Restore the power himself
Certify the work complete and that all staff, tools and materials are clear of the track
Send the first train through to check
questions.explain: Certification comes first: work complete, men and material counted and clear — then hand-back can begin.

questions.q: Power may be restored only when:
options: Both Person-in-Charge (PIC) and Operations Control Centre (OCC) confirm — after the PIC's certification that the line is clear and fit
The PIC alone decides silently
The time window expires
The first train is waiting
questions.explain: Restoration follows certification and joint Person-in-Charge (PIC) + Operations Control Centre (OCC) confirmation — never the clock alone.

questions.q: In what order are the Permit to Work (PTW) and earths dealt with at the end of work?
options: Power restored → earths removed → PTW cancelled → Person-in-Charge (PIC) certifies
Earths removed → PIC certifies → power restored → PTW cancelled
PTW cancelled → power restored → earths removed → PIC certifies
PIC certifies clear → PTW is cancelled → earths are removed → power is restored
questions.explain: The closing steps run in exact reverse discipline: certify, cancel the permit, remove earths, restore power.

questions.q: After hand-back, how may the first train be run, as prescribed?
options: At full line speed immediately
At caution speed, after any trial/inspection as prescribed
Without informing the operator
Only after one hour in all cases
questions.explain: Hand-back may include a trial/inspection run and a first train at caution speed before normal service resumes.

questions.q: Handing back possession early because work finished sooner is:
options: Forbidden in all circumstances
Allowed only after Person-in-Charge (PIC) certification and formal hand-back to Operations Control Centre (OCC)
Done by a phone call to the driver
Automatic when staff leave
questions.explain: Early hand-back is fine — but only through the same formal certification and hand-back, never informally.

questions.q: What is the absolute rule about entering the track during live (traffic) hours?
options: Entry is allowed if you are quick
Entry is allowed in uniform
No track entry in live hours without proper authority
Entry is allowed at night
questions.explain: Live hours plus no authority equals a prohibited and potentially fatal combination.

questions.q: Scenario: The power has been switched off for your section but earthing is not yet applied. Can staff start work?
options: No — switching off alone does not make the wire safe; earthing and Permit to Work (PTW) must follow first
Yes, switched off means safe
Yes, if they wear gloves
Yes, for a few minutes only
questions.explain: This is the classic exam trap: isolation without earthing is incomplete protection.

questions.q: Scenario: A worker wants to enter the possession to collect a forgotten tool after hand-back. He should:
options: Enter quickly since he knows the site
Ask the first train to slow down for him
Enter from the platform end quietly
Not enter — the possession is over; entry now needs fresh authority through Operations Control Centre (OCC)/Person-in-Charge (PIC) channels
questions.explain: After hand-back the track is live railway again. The forgotten tool waits for a new authorised access.

questions.q: What do scotches and stop boards do in a possession?
options: Decorate the worksite
Hold the tools
Physically mark and block the limits so trains cannot enter the protected section
Show the staff where to stand
questions.explain: Scotches/stop boards are physical protection at the limits, backing up the signals and blocks.

questions.q: Why must tools and materials be 'accounted for' before hand-back?
options: So nothing is left on the track to foul or damage the first train
For the stores register only
So staff can be paid
It is not actually required
questions.explain: A spanner left on the rail can derail a train — counting men and material is a safety step, not clerical work.

questions.q: The traffic/power plan and caution orders for a planned possession are issued:
options: After the work is over
Only if the work is delayed
Verbally at the last minute
In advance, as part of the planning and sanction stage
questions.explain: Planning includes the traffic and power plan plus caution orders, all issued before the possession begins.

questions.q: Which sequence is correct inside the protection-and-isolation steps?
options: Issue Permit to Work (PTW) → protect → earth → isolate
Protect the section (signals at danger, points secured) → isolate power → earth the Overhead Equipment (OHE) → issue PTW
Earth → isolate → protect → issue PTW
Isolate → issue PTW → earth → protect
questions.explain: First keep trains out, then kill the power, then earth it, then permit the work — in that order.

questions.q: A possession's limits and time are best described as:
options: Flexible, extendable by the Person-in-Charge (PIC) alone
Defined and fixed — work stays within the protected limits and the permitted time only
Decided by the workers on site
Unlimited once granted
questions.explain: The Person-in-Charge (PIC) controls staff and tools strictly inside the granted limits and time window.

questions.q: Who resumes normal working after hand-back?
options: The Person-in-Charge (PIC)
The power controller alone
Operations Control Centre (OCC), once possession is formally handed back
The first train's operator
questions.explain: Operations Control Centre (OCC) granted the possession and Operations Control Centre (OCC) resumes normal working after formal hand-back.

questions.q: Scenario: During work, the Person-in-Charge (PIC) loses radio contact with Operations Control Centre (OCC). The safe action is:
options: Stop or secure the work as per procedure and re-establish communication — the communication check must be maintained
Continue working silently till the end
Send a worker along the track to Operations Control Centre (OCC)
Ignore it; communication is optional
questions.explain: Communication with Operations Control Centre (OCC) is a condition of the possession; losing it means securing the work until contact returns.

questions.q: Why is the Permit to Work (PTW) issued only AFTER earthing, never before?
options: Because of office timing
Because the Person-in-Charge (PIC) arrives late
It can be issued any time
Because the permit certifies the section is proved dead and safe to touch — which only earthing establishes
questions.explain: The Permit to Work (PTW) is a safety certificate, not a formality: it can only certify safety that has actually been created.

questions.q: What happens to signals protecting the section during hand-back?
options: They stay at danger forever
Workers remove them casually
Protection is removed in order, as part of the formal hand-back, before normal service resumes
They are removed before the Person-in-Charge (PIC) certifies
questions.explain: Protection comes off in the prescribed order during hand-back — after certification, never before it.

questions.q: A trial or inspection after hand-back is done:
options: As prescribed, before normal service fully resumes
Never — trains just start
Only if passengers demand it
By passengers on the first train
questions.explain: Where prescribed, a trial/inspection run proves the section before normal service resumes.

questions.q: Which statement about adjacent-line working is correct?
options: The adjacent line needs no thought
Trains on the adjacent line protect themselves
Work can spread onto it freely
If work can foul the adjacent line, precautions for that line must be taken as prescribed
questions.explain: Fouling risk does not stop at the possession boundary — the adjacent line gets its own precautions.

questions.q: The single most dangerous misunderstanding about a switched-off Overhead Equipment (OHE) is:
options: Believing it needs a Permit to Work (PTW)
Believing switched off means safe to touch — without earthing it may still be live or become live
Believing the Person-in-Charge (PIC) is in charge
Believing Operations Control Centre (OCC) must be informed
questions.explain: Isolation can fail or be reversed; earthing is what proves and keeps the wire dead. Treat Overhead Equipment (OHE) as live until earthed and permitted.

questions.q: A Permit to Work (PTW) for work on or near the track may be received only by:
options: Any worker present at the site
A competent, authorised person (the Person-in-Charge) who has been briefed and is named for that work
The youngest member of the team
A contractor's supervisor from another site
questions.explain: The Permit to Work (PTW) transfers a defined safety responsibility to one named, competent person. If anyone could receive it, nobody would truly own the safety of the worksite.

questions.q: Even after a section is isolated at the switching points, local earths are applied at the worksite itself mainly to protect against:
options: Rain
Accidental re-energisation and induced voltage from adjacent live sections appearing at the work point
Dust on the wire
Theft of the wire
questions.explain: Isolation happens far away; danger can still reach the worksite through a switching mistake or induction from a neighbouring live section. A local earth at the work point clamps the wire to earth potential exactly where people are touching it.

questions.q: An isolated Overhead Equipment (OHE) section running parallel to a live section can still show a dangerous voltage because of:
options: Static from passengers' clothes
Electromagnetic induction from the adjacent live conductor
The colour of the wire
Battery leakage from trains
questions.explain: Parallel live conductors induce voltage in a dead conductor — this is why 'switched off' is never treated as 'safe' until the section is earthed at the worksite.

questions.q: Engineering possessions are normally planned and published in advance (for example in a weekly possession programme) mainly so that:
options: Staff can choose their favourite shifts
Operations, maintenance and power-supply teams can coordinate traffic regulation, isolation and manpower before the night of the work
The public can watch the work
No approval is needed later
questions.explain: A possession touches trains, power, signals and people at once. Publishing it in advance lets every team plan around the same window — an unplanned possession is an emergency exception, not the method.

questions.q: Before the Person-in-Charge hands back a possession, he must account for:
options: Only the senior staff
Every person, and also tools and materials — nothing and nobody may be left on or near the line
Only the machines
Only the paperwork
questions.explain: Hand-back certifies the line is fit for trains. A forgotten tool on the track or a missing worker is as dangerous as unfinished work, so people, tools and materials are all counted and confirmed clear.
